summary: Weekly POC sync focusing on benchmark comparisons versus customer's current baseline provider. Redwood showed improvements on p50/p95 latency for the smaller model variant and comparable throughput at matched cost with batching and KV cache. Customer flagged variability during sustained bursts and raised networking/VPC questions for Private deployment. Agreed next steps: share logs, run additional staging load test, and align on VPC peering call.
topics: Benchmark overview: p50/p95/p99 latency vs baseline
Throughput / concurrency behavior and cost normalization
Configuration details: batching, KV cache, quantization variant
questions: Can Redwood guarantee p95 latency under 220ms at 1k qps?
How does KV cache warmup affect steady-state latency?
Is dedicated capacity required to eliminate the burst variability we saw?
header: Date: 2026-06-16, Time: 10:30 AM UTC, Duration: 45m; Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Daniel Wu (Redwood CSM), Michael Torres (Nimbus AI CTO), Sara Lee (Nimbus ML Eng), Jenna Park (Nimbus SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick agenda—benchmarks review, discuss variability, then next steps for the VPC test. um, priya will run through the numbers.
[00:18] Priya Kapoor: hi all. okay so, we re-ran the benchmark this week with the same request set you shared, thanks Michael, and we normalized cost to your baseline provider so the comparison is apples-to-apples. main takeaways — p50 improved by about 18% on the small variant, p95 improved 12%, throughput at equivalent cost was within 5%.
[00:40] Michael Torres: cool. when you say small variant is that the 7B quantized model? and were you using Redwood Dedicated or hosted for this run?
[00:52] Priya Kapoor: good question. this run used Redwood hosted on our optimized instances, model is 7B-quant-4 (the quantized 4-bit path), with KV cache enabled for repeated prefixes. we also tested the 13B variant but raw latency there was similar to baseline for p95, but cost was higher so not as favorable.
[01:12] Sara Lee: are the numbers you have per-request or per-token? like what's the tokenization overhead?
[01:20] Priya Kapoor: we report end-to-end per-request latencies; tokenization overhead is included. per-token breakdown in the spreadsheet — we'll share the logs — shows tokenization adds ~8-12ms on average for your request mix.
[01:34] Jenna Park: we saw a couple spikes in the telemetry you sent—around minute 18 and 29, there's a p95 jump. what caused that?
[01:42] Priya Kapoor: yeah so there was a sustained burst test where concurrency hit a sustained 1.2k qps for about 45s; our autoscaling bumped, but KV cache hit-rate dipped during scale events which causes transient higher p95 until caches warmed. also, a couple requests routed to a fallback model variant during capacity pressure.
[02:03] Michael Torres: fallback to a different model? we want predictable behavior — fallback is concerning from a quality standpoint. can you guarantee the same model?
[02:12] Alex Chen: short answer: we can pin to a model/variant to avoid fallback, at the expense of committed capacity or slightly higher cost. recommendation is to use reserved Dedicated for strict SLAs. for the POC, we can pin a small pool to avoid model swaps during your load tests.
[02:30] Sara Lee: pinned pool sounds good. but how much of a cost uplift are we talking?
[02:36] Alex Chen: depends on size. rough thumb: dedicated reserved pool to handle sustained 1k qps on 7B-quant is about X% over our burstable hosted pricing — we'll send a detailed cost sheet.
[02:48] Priya Kapoor: back to the benchmark — we also tried aggressive batching, which improved tokens/sec by about 22% at a slight p50 increase ~10ms. for low-latency workloads we used small batch sizes and continuous batching to avoid tail latencies.
[03:04] Michael Torres: when you say continuous batching, is that adaptive? do we control the batch window?
[03:10] Priya Kapoor: yes it's workload-aware batching, we set a max wait of 10ms for the runs Garcia — sorry — the setting was 10ms, and that was the sweet spot for your workload. you can tune wait window and max batch size in config.
[03:22] Sara Lee: what's the KV cache hit rate during steady-state?
[03:25] Priya Kapoor: around 76% steady-state for your request distribution, but during the burst it dropped to ~42% because cold replicas came up. that explains some of the transient p95 jumps.
[03:36] Jenna Park: is the KV cache local to the GPU or shared? we need to know networking implications for the private deployment.
[03:42] Priya Kapoor: KV cache in hosted is local to the serving node, we do prefix caching in memory. for Private/Dedicated we can provision a shared cache layer or warm-on-start to avoid cold starts — Jenna we should follow up with configuration recommendations for your topology.
[03:55] Michael Torres: okay. can you walk through the normalized throughput numbers vs our baseline provider? i want explicit p50/p95 and tokens/sec.
[04:03] Priya Kapoor: sure, quick summary: baseline provider (your current) — p50 110ms, p95 340ms, tokens/sec 18k at the normalized cost. Redwood hosted — p50 90ms, p95 300ms, tokens/sec 19k. with aggressive batching tokens/sec hit 22k but p95 was ~320ms. these are median of 6 runs. full table in the sheet.
[04:33] Michael Torres: hmm p95 improvement is nice but still worried about the 300ms around p95. our target is p95 < 220ms. can Redwood meet that?
[04:41] Alex Chen: that's one of the success criteria we can aim for. to get p95 down to 220ms at 1k qps we'd recommend either moving to dedicated reserved capacity or using a lighter model variant plus more aggressive kv caching and batching tradeoffs. need to run targeted tuning.
[04:58] Sara Lee: any quantization artifacts observed? output quality regressions?
[05:03] Priya Kapoor: qualitatively none for the test prompts you gave — we ran the eval set you shared, rouge/accuracy delta within 1-2% for 7B-quant-4. for safety we can run your longer eval suite on the 7B and 13B variants.
[05:18] Michael Torres: sounds good. about the variability — is it mostly cache warmup or could it be network egress throttling on your side?
[05:27] Priya Kapoor: primarily cache warmup and autoscale timing plus a handful of requests routed to a fallback variant during peak. network egress is unlikely — we monitored network metrics and didn't see bottlenecks.
[05:38] Michael Torres: ok. Jenna, from SRE perspective do you think pinned dedicated is feasible for us?
[05:44] Jenna Park: yes, we can evaluate. key question is VPC peering and IP ranges — we need to audit firewall and egress policies. also want to test MTU and any path MTU issues.
[05:56] Daniel Wu: we can set up a VPC networking deep-dive next week; Alex, Priya, we'll bring the infra folks.
[06:02] Alex Chen: perfect. timeline wise, we will share the detailed per-token logs and the config snippet for batching and kv cache by tomorrow EOD. Michael — could you run one more staged test with a 4k short burst pattern and share the telemetry?
[06:14] Michael Torres: yep can do. we'll run that on staging and upload the logs. target for that is Friday the 22nd.
[06:20] Priya Kapoor: also a note — for the run today we used our conservative autoscale policy. if you want more aggressive scale up we can change the policy to spin up replicas faster but that will increase cost.
[06:31] Sara Lee: what's the worst-case cold-start p95 we saw?
[06:35] Priya Kapoor: worst cold-start p95 in the tests was ~620ms but that's during full cold scale from 0. in production we recommend keeping a small hot pool to avoid that.
[06:47] Michael Torres: for the POC, we want reproducible numbers. let's pin the model and reserve a small pool so warmup isn't a confounder.
[06:56] Alex Chen: agreed, we'll provision a pinned pool for your next run. cost sheet will show the delta.
[07:05] Jenna Park: on compliance — we need SOC2 and encryption-at-rest details, can you attach the security docs in the next email?
[07:11] Daniel Wu: yep we will send SOC2 and KMS/HSM integration notes after the call.
[07:16] Sara Lee: quick question — you mentioned fallback model variant earlier. is it a smaller quantized model or lower quality family? want clarity because output quality changes matter for us.
[07:26] Priya Kapoor: by fallback I meant a compatible model family in the catalog that fits resource constraints — typically a smaller quantized variant. we'll share the mapping we used in test so you can see exact model ids.
[07:37] Michael Torres: thanks. any concerns about data residency or logs? we have to ensure no PII leaves our VPC during private runs.
[07:44] Alex Chen: for Private deployments all traffic stays in your VPC; logs can be siloed to your account and we support customer-managed KMS. we'll document exactly what telemetry is sent during hosted tests.
[07:56] Priya Kapoor: ok moving toward wrap — action items: we'll upload the full spreadsheet and token-level traces; Redwood SE to provide config snippet; Nimbus to run extra burst test; schedule VPC networking call.
[08:10] Michael Torres: good recap. any blockers on Redwood side for setup?
[08:15] Alex Chen: none. we just need the CIDR and SRE contact for the VPC peering and staging credentials for the next load test.
[08:24] Jenna Park: sending CIDR after the call.
[08:28] Daniel Wu: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite for the infra deep-dive.
[08:34] Michael Torres: thanks all, appreciate the improvements so far — we'll dig into the sheet and get the staged run scheduled.
[08:39] Alex Chen: thanks, talk soon.
[45:00] (call ended)
